## Example datasets

The module includes example datasets derived from published studies for testing and learning purposes. References for the original data sources are provided with each dataset.

They are available from the jamovi menu in the upper-left corner:

**Open → Data Library → PGM**

## Basic structure

Data should be provided in long format, with one row per observation.

At minimum, an analysis requires:

- one numeric response variable;
- one numeric time or age variable.

Additional variables may be supplied as:

- fixed-effect predictors;
- random-effects grouping variables;
- residual-correlation grouping variables.

## Simple structure

For an ordinary nonlinear model:

| time | response |
|-----:|---------:|
| 1 | 12.4 |
| 2 | 18.9 |
| 3 | 27.5 |

## Repeated-measures structure

For repeated measurements, each experimental unit should have a stable grouping identifier.

| subject | treatment | time | response |
|:--------|:----------|-----:|---------:|
| A01 | Control | 1 | 12.4 |
| A01 | Control | 2 | 18.9 |
| A01 | Control | 3 | 27.5 |
| A02 | Treated | 1 | 11.8 |
| A02 | Treated | 2 | 19.7 |
| A02 | Treated | 3 | 29.1 |

Here, `treatment` may be used as a fixed-effect predictor and `subject` as a random-effects or residual-correlation grouping variable.

## Variable requirements

### Response

The response must be numeric and should represent a process compatible with the selected growth equation.

Examples include body mass, length, concentration, plant height, biomass, or cumulative production.

### Time

Time must be numeric.

Examples include:

- age in days;
- age in weeks;
- hours after inoculation;
- days after planting.

The unit of time determines the numerical scale of time-dependent model parameters and derivative quantities.

### Fixed-effect predictors

Fixed effects represent systematic changes in one or more growth parameters.

Predictors may be categorical or continuous.

Categorical predictors must contain at least two observed levels in the data actually used for the fit. Interaction terms also require sufficient observations in the relevant combinations of predictor levels.

For each growth parameter, the selected fixed-effect terms define a separate parameter model.

For example,

$$
\log(K)
=
\beta_0+
\beta_1 X+
\beta_2 Z+
\beta_3 XZ
$$

represents main effects of $X$ and $Z$ and their interaction on the internally estimated $K$ parameter.

### Random-effects grouping variables

Random-effects grouping variables identify units among which one or more growth parameters are allowed to vary.

Examples include:

- subject;
- animal;
- nest;
- batch;
- experimental unit.

Several grouping levels may be used when they form a nested hierarchy.

For example, using the Imperial Shag dataset included with PGM [@svagelj2021]:

`nestID`  
`chickID`

may represent chicks nested within nests when each chick belongs to one nest.

Composite grouping terms may also be created explicitly. A term such as

`species:replicate`

represents the unique combinations of species and replicate.

The current implementation requires a unique nested hierarchy. Crossed random-effects structures that cannot be represented as a unique nesting order are not supported.

### Correlation Groups

Correlation Groups define the units within which an AR(1) or CAR(1) residual correlation structure is applied.

When more than one variable is selected, they define an ordered grouping hierarchy from outer to inner level.

For example:

`nestID / chickID`

models residual correlation within chicks nested in nests.

Correlation Groups are conceptually distinct from random effects. They may coincide with random-effects groups, but they serve a different statistical purpose.

## Missing observations

For each model setup, PGM uses complete observations for:

- the selected response;
- time;
- all selected fixed-effect predictors;
- all selected random-effects grouping variables;
- all selected Correlation Groups.

Rows containing missing values in any required variable are excluded from that fit.

This can be particularly important when predictors have structurally missing values. After complete-case filtering, a categorical predictor may be left with only one observed level, in which case its effect cannot be estimated.

## Factor levels and estimability

Unused factor levels are removed before GNLS or NLME estimation.

PGM checks whether categorical fixed-effect predictors retain at least two observed levels and whether the resulting fixed-effects design matrix has full column rank.

Empty combinations of factor levels, redundant terms, or perfect collinearity may make a requested effect or interaction non-estimable.

## Measurement schedule

Discrete AR(1) correlation is most naturally used when observations follow an approximately equally spaced measurement schedule.

For irregularly spaced measurements, continuous-time CAR(1) is generally more appropriate because correlation is modeled using the actual temporal distance.

## Data coverage

A nonlinear growth curve should ideally contain observations from the early, rapidly growing, and late portions of the trajectory.

If the observed data do not adequately cover the upper part of the curve, the asymptotic parameter may be weakly identified and highly uncertain.

Early or truncated datasets may produce:

- unstable asymptotes and geometric descriptors;
- strong parameter correlations;
- wide confidence intervals;
- implausible extrapolation;
- convergence failures.

When the asymptote is scientifically known or deliberately constrained, PGM allows a positive fixed asymptotic value to be supplied in the Model Setup.

Predictions beyond the observed time range should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously.
